title: Experimental transplants reveal cryptogam responses to microclimate buffering across a boreal forest‐management gradient
content:
Maintaining canopy cover and structural continuity is important for buffering cryptogams against microclimatic stress. Conservation of old, closed-canopy stands provides the strongest protection for sensitive bryophytes and lichens, while retention patches can partially reduce harvesting impacts but do not fully reproduce old-forest conditions. Retention planning should therefore prioritise sufficient canopy cover and structural continuity, especially where late-successional and thermally sensitive bryophytes and lichens are conservation targets.


Abstract

Understorey cryptogams are fundamental to forest biodiversity and ecosystem functioning, yet their persistence is increasingly threatened as climate warming and forest harvesting expose them to hotter, drier microclimates. Because stand structure can buffer below-canopy temperatures and humidity, an important management challenge is to determine whether retention forestry can maintain microclimatic conditions that support sensitive cryptogams. We experimentally transplanted four bryophytes (Hylocomiadelphus triquetrus, Hylocomium splendens, Neckera oligocarpa, Hylocomiastrum umbratum) and one lichen (Lobaria pulmonaria) across a management gradient of clearcuts, retention patches and old forests in the cool, relatively dry inland boreal climate of central Sweden. We modelled seasonal growth and vitality in relation to forest management, microclimate, stand structure and thermal deviation from occurrence-derived realised thermal reference conditions. Old forests most effectively buffered microclimates and supported the highest growth with the smallest decline in vitality. Retention patches reduced performance declines relative to clearcuts in microclimate-sensitive taxa, but provided little additional benefit for tolerant species whose growth was maintained across treatments. Growth and vitality provided complementary indicators of performance: growth followed quadratic relationships with thermal deviation, declining under both colder- and warmer-than-reference conditions, whereas vitality declined primarily under warmer-than-reference conditions. Compared with old forests, performance in clearcuts and retention patches was more strongly influenced by microclimatic and structural drivers. Synthesis and applications. Maintaining canopy cover and structural continuity is important for buffering cryptogams against microclimatic stress. Conservation of old, closed-canopy stands provides the strongest protection for sensitive bryophytes and lichens, while retention patches can partially reduce harvesting impacts but do not fully reproduce old-forest conditions. Retention planning should therefore prioritise sufficient canopy cover and structural continuity, especially where late-successional and thermally sensitive bryophytes and lichens are conservation targets.
